narrative: The model estimates a 64% chance that you will leave your job. Because this is above the level used to treat someone as likely to leave, you are denied a promotion at this time. The most influential signal was your total years of experience, and it actually pointed toward staying: your 1–5 years is the most common range among employees predicted to stay. The second most influential signal was that you have other job opportunities. That pushed strongly toward leaving, because only about 23% of employees predicted to stay reported other opportunities. The third signal was your sector; being in “other” also pushed toward leaving, since medical and education sectors are more common among stayers. Together, those leaving signals and other retention-risk factors outweighed the experience signal. To improve the outlook, you and your manager should discuss your career path and any outside opportunities, clarify what promotion would require, and address retention drivers such as pay satisfaction, recognition, training, benefits, and job stability. A clear development and retention plan would help show whether your likelihood of staying can be reduced before promotion is reconsidered.
